Issued at 530 AM CDT Wed Jul 29 2026

Upper level ridge extends from the Southern Rockies through 
Northern High Plains early this morning. North Dakota lies 
between high pressure over Wisconsin and a surface trough over 
central Montana. Ground-truth reports indicate smoke remains 
present in the near- surface layer across northern North Dakota,
and on its own has been reducing visibility as low as 5 miles. 
Particulates from the smoke have provided sufficient 
condensation nuclei for patchy fog to develop in low-lying areas
of north central North Dakota early this morning. The fog is 
not expected to be nearly as impactful as 24 hours ago, but 
there have been brief observations of quarter mile visibility 
from western Bottineau to northern Ward Counties. Any fog should
burn off by mid morning, but near-surface smoke could persist 
through the day, if not longer. A mention of patchy smoke was 
maintained in the forecast through this afternoon, with 
confidence beyond the afternoon remaining low.

Today is expected to be the hottest day of the work week as the
thermal ridge once again points into the western Dakotas. The 
NBM suspiciously increased its 50th percentile high temperature 
projections by a few to several degrees, which seems 
inconsistent with all other previous and current guidance. We 
trended our high temperature forecast closer to the maximum of 
NBM/HRRR hourly guidance, which gives a more reasonable forecast
of around 95 to 100 across most of western and central North 
Dakota, and is much more consistent with previous forecasts over
the past few days that had shown little to no change. The 
hottest forecast temperatures and heat indices are focused over 
the Missouri River Valley, and also extend south to the I-94 
corridor west of the river. A Heat Advisory has been issued for 
these areas, in effect from noon to 8 PM CDT.

Forecast confidence in convective evolution and intensity this 
afternoon through tonight is not that high. An inverted lee 
trough is forecast along the ND/MT by mid afternoon. CAMs are 
consistent that there will be enough forcing from surface 
convergence, low level frontogenesis, and weak shortwave energy 
ejecting off the Northern Rockies to initiate deep moist 
convection along the surface boundary by mid to late afternoon. 
Despite hot temperatures and dewpoints only favored to mix down 
into the lower to mid 50s, model soundings reveal a skinny CAPE 
profile with very high LFCs at around 600 mb. Differences in mid
to late afternoon buoyancy projections range from as high as 
2500 J/kg SBCAPE in the RAP to as low as 500 J/kg in the HREF 
mean MUCAPE. Think closer to 1000 J/kg is the most likely 
outcome, which is still sufficient for severe storms but lower 
than previously anticipated. The deep layer shear forecast has 
also weakened in the most recent model guidance, with only 
around 25- 35 kts in the 0-6 km layer, highest in northwest 
North Dakota. Dry- air entrainment and residual CIN also remain 
a concern for convective development and sustainment. These 
limiting factors are seemingly reflected in CAMs' UH output, 
with HREF neighborhood probabilities of UH greater than 75 
m^2/s^2 only reaching 10 percent, and only that high in 
northwest and north central North Dakota. Previous forecast 
thinking on a favored storm mode of linear north to discrete 
south remains valid as far as vector orientation is concerned, 
but CAMs' reflectivity is more indicative of a mixed/cluster 
mode with splitting supercells (which modeled hodographs do 
confirm is a possible outcome). Because of the inverted-v 
thermodynamic profile, damaging wind is the most likely severe 
hazard. Large hail is still possible with discrete storms, but 
the decrease of forecast CAPE and shear has prompted us to lower
our most likely maximum hail size forecast to ping pong balls. 
The tornado risk in northwest North Dakota, which was already 
low to begin with, appears to have lowered even further. But 
because there is still potential for a triple-point axis, and 
model hodographs at Crosby have actually switched from crosswise
to streamwise vorticity in the 0-1 km layer, will maintain the 
mention of a possible tornado in far northwest North Dakota for 
now.

CAMs remain inconsistent on convective evolution into central 
North Dakota during the overnight hours. The risk for severe 
storms is likely to end by around midnight, but one to a few 
clusters of storms could persist through the night. On Thursday,
a deeper shortwave is forecast to cross the Northern Plains and
produce widespread showers and thunderstorms, especially across
the southern half of the state. Enough CAPE and shear may be

likely to remain elevated. The greatest concern from
